passage:
After dinner at home, Anand looked up from the sofa. "Karthik, why are you checking your phone every five minutes?"
"It's the match, Anand bhaiya. I've got a bit riding on it."
"A bit?"
"Just a small bet. On the app."
"You said that last month. And the month before."
Karthik looked away. "I'm about to win back what I lost."
"How much did you lose?"
Silence. Then, "More than my stipend."
"Karthik."
"I know. I know. Every time I lose, I think the next one will fix it. And when I win, I want to bet more."
"That sounds like a trap."
"It is." His voice cracked. "I don't know how to stop."
Anand sat down beside his younger brother. "Okay. We'll find help. The counselling centre does this. I'll come."
Karthik nodded, and deleted the app while Anand watched.

qa.q: How much had Karthik lost?
qa.a: He had lost more than his stipend.

qa.q: What does Karthik's cracking voice reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: It reveals he feels trapped and ashamed, knowing the betting is out of control but not knowing how to stop.

qa.q: What made Anand's response helpful?
qa.a: He named the pattern calmly, didn't shame Karthik, and offered to go with him to get professional help.

qa.q: How might Anand feel, as Karthik's older brother, hearing about the losses?
qa.a: Anand is likely worried and shaken, but he stays calm and offers to come along, so Karthik feels able to accept help instead of hiding.

grounding: It shows a young man recognising a gambling dependence loop and taking a first step to exit it with his older brother's help.

passage: I didn't think gaming could be a problem until it was. I'm Shreya. In second year, I started playing online after classes. Then through dinner. Then through the night. I told myself I could stop anytime. I skipped my brother Siddharth's birthday call because I was mid-match. That's when I felt sick about it. I tried to quit on my own, but I'd last two days, feel restless, and go back. It was like my brain needed it. Finally I told a college counsellor. She helped me see the loop: stress, play, relief, guilt, more stress. We made a plan with blocked hours and things to do instead, like evening walks with a friend. I still play sometimes. But I choose when.

qa.q: Whose birthday call did Shreya skip?
qa.a: She skipped her brother Siddharth's birthday call.

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel sick after skipping the call?
qa.a: She realised gaming was pushing out the people she loved, which made her see the habit was out of control.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Shreya exit the loop?
qa.a: She helped her understand the cycle of stress, play, relief and guilt, and plan blocked hours and alternative activities.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about Shreya's change?
qa.a: Siddharth may have been hurt by the missed call; now that Shreya chooses when she plays, there may be more room for calls with him.

grounding: A young woman reflects on a gaming dependence loop and how she exited it with professional help.

passage:
College counsellor's note:
Jatin, 21, came in after his friend Gopika urged him to. He said he drinks "a bit" most nights to fall asleep and to cope with stress about exams. Over the last few months he's needed more to feel the same, and he feels anxious and shaky when he skips it. He missed two exams. He was defensive at first, saying "everyone drinks in college." When I asked what he wanted his life to look like in a year, he became quiet and said, "Not like this."
We discussed the cycle of stress, drinking, worse sleep and more stress. I referred him to the campus doctor and a support group. Next steps: weekly sessions. He asked if Gopika could come to the first support meeting.

qa.q: How many exams did Jatin miss?
qa.a: He missed two exams.

qa.q: What does Jatin's "Not like this" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests that under his defensiveness, he was unhappy with where his drinking was taking him and wanted to change.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that was helpful?
qa.a: The counsellor didn't argue with his defensiveness but asked about his future, explained the cycle, and referred him to a doctor and support group.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel when Jatin asks Gopika to come to the support meeting?
qa.a: Gopika might feel relieved and trusted, glad the urging led Jatin to get help.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young man recognising an alcohol dependence loop and starting professional help.

passage:
Friday night
Lost again. Not a huge amount, but it was my mess money for the month, and I only meant to play 'one round' of that online card game after dinner. I keep doing the same thing: lose, feel sick, play again to win it back, win a little, feel great, play more. It's a loop and I'm the hamster in the wheel. Tarun saw me on my phone at 2 am last week and asked if I was okay. I lied and said I was chatting. Today I told him the truth. He didn't lecture. He just said, 'Let's deal with it, Nilesh.' So: uninstalled the app, gave Tarun my debit card to keep for now, and tomorrow I'm calling Maa, even though I'm dreading it. Tarun also found a helpline for gambling problems. I saved the number. Scared. Also lighter.

qa.q: What money did Nilesh lose?
qa.a: The mess money for the month.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel at the end of the entry, and what shows it?
qa.a: Scared and lighter at once; Nilesh dreads calling Maa, yet telling Tarun and taking steps has eased the weight of the secret.

qa.q: Which steps help Nilesh break the loop?
qa.a: Removing the app, putting the debit card out of easy reach, planning to tell family and saving a helpline number give barriers and support instead of willpower alone.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Nilesh told him the truth?
qa.a: Perhaps a little hurt about the earlier lie, but mostly concerned and glad to be trusted, which is why he said, 'Let's deal with it.' 🤍

grounding: A diary entry shows a student recognising a gambling dependence loop and taking first steps to exit it with support.

passage: Behind the counter of her father's hardware shop in Karad, Lakshmi kept her phone under the ledger. The card game started as ten minutes between customers. Win a little, feel bright. Lose a little, play one more to win it back. By July she was topping up from the shop's cash drawer and writing the gaps in pencil so she could "fix them later". Jahnavi, her school friend, came in for nails and saw her hands shaking as a round ended. "Lakshmi, you're not even looking at me." That night Lakshmi added up the pencil gaps and felt sick. She told Jahnavi first, then, with Jahnavi sitting beside her, her father. He was silent a long time. Then he said, "We'll fix the drawer together. And you'll see someone." Next morning they went to the counsellor at the district hospital, and Lakshmi deleted the game in the waiting room.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi keep her phone?
qa.a: Under the ledger.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when she added up the pencil gaps?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt sick with shame and fear once she saw how much had gone from the drawer.

qa.q: What steps helped Lakshmi start to break the loop?
qa.a: Telling Jahnavi and then her father that same night, going to the counsellor at the district hospital, and deleting the game removed the secrecy and the easy access.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's father have felt during his long silence?
qa.a: He was probably shocked and hurt, then worried for her, choosing to fix things together rather than only punish.

grounding: In a small town, a young woman caught in a gambling loop tells her friend and father and starts getting help.

passage: In Jana's first year at university in Brno, every evening ended the same way. A beer to "switch off" after lectures, then two, then messages she regretted in the morning. By spring she needed a drink before any seminar where she had to speak. One Sunday Ada, her flatmate, found the empty bottles in the recycling and didn't lecture. She asked, "When did it stop being fun?" Jana opened her mouth to joke and couldn't. "Maybe November," she said. "I don't know how to talk in class without it anymore." That frightened her more than any hangover. That evening, with Ada beside her, she called the student support line. The adviser listened, told her she had done the right thing by calling, and booked her with a counsellor for Monday. Ada offered evening swims together instead of the drinks.

qa.q: Where did Ada find the empty bottles?
qa.a: In the recycling.

qa.q: Why was Jana frightened by her own answer to Ada?
qa.a: Jana felt frightened realising she no longer knew how to speak in class without drinking, a sign the habit had become a need.

qa.q: What makes this a realistic start to leaving the loop?
qa.a: Calling the support line the same day brought in a professional, the counsellor appointment adds ongoing help, and swims with Ada replace the evening habit.

qa.q: How might Ada have felt asking 'When did it stop being fun?'
qa.a: Ada was probably worried but careful, choosing a gentle question over a lecture so Jana could answer honestly.

grounding: A student abroad recognises a drinking dependence loop when a flatmate asks gently, and seeks help that day.

passage: The attendance notice said sixty-one percent. Harsha folded it into quarters before walking into the campus wellness centre. Ishita, a final-year volunteer at the front desk, noticed his red eyes and offered him water while he waited. "I play one match at night to relax," he told her, almost defensively. "Then it's four a.m. Then I miss the nine o'clock class. Then I feel rubbish, so I play again." Ishita nodded. Advice wasn't her job. She wrote down the loop he had just described, word for word, and handed it to him. "Tell the counsellor exactly this. It's clearer than most people manage." Inside, the counsellor listened, and together they made a plan: the console left at his cousin's flat for the semester, a sports club at night, and weekly check-ins. Harsha came out and gave Ishita a small, embarrassed thumbs-up.

qa.q: What attendance did the notice show?
qa.a: Sixty-one percent.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling while describing the loop?
qa.a: Harsha felt defensive and ashamed, feeling rubbish after missed classes yet pulled back into playing.

qa.q: Which parts of the plan target the loop directly?
qa.a: Leaving the console at his cousin's flat removes the trigger, the night-time sports club fills that slot, and weekly check-ins keep him on track.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel seeing the embarrassed thumbs-up?
qa.a: Ishita would likely feel quietly glad that writing down his own words helped him speak to the counsellor.

grounding: At a campus wellness centre, a student describes his gaming loop and makes a plan with a counsellor to exit it.

passage:
Dear Chandrika,
You asked why I've been off the fantasy betting app. I want to be honest with you.
It started as fun: small bets on cricket with friends. Then I was checking it every hour. When I lost, I'd bet more to win it back. When I won, I felt amazing for a minute, then wanted more. I hid it from everyone.
Last month I borrowed from my roommate to cover a loss. That's when I got scared.
I told my brother. He helped me delete the app, block payments on my card, and find a counsellor who works with gambling problems. I've been off it for three weeks.
Some days I still want to check. I call you or go for a walk instead.
Thanks for asking. It helped to say it.
Lavanya

qa.q: Whom did Lavanya borrow from to cover a loss?
qa.a: The roommate.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling after borrowing to cover a loss?
qa.a: Lavanya felt scared, seeing how out of control the betting had become.

qa.q: What steps helped Lavanya exit the loop?
qa.a: Telling the brother, deleting the app, blocking card payments and seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Chandrika probably feels trusted and wants to keep supporting Lavanya.

grounding: A young adult writes to a friend about recognising and exiting a betting dependence loop.

passage:
You want to know about my gaming? I'm Parul. Okay.
In second year, I'd play from ten at night till five in the morning. Online team games. I'd tell myself one more match, every match. If I stopped, I felt restless and irritable. I skipped classes. I lied to my parents about marks.
My friend Parveen noticed first. She said, "You look grey." I laughed it off.
Then I failed two papers. I sat in my room and couldn't even open the game; I just cried.
I went to the student counselling centre that week. The counsellor explained the loop: stress, game, relief, guilt, more stress. We made a plan. Deleted the game from my laptop. Played football instead. Told my parents the truth.
It took months. I still play sometimes, but not at night.

qa.q: How many papers did Parul fail?
qa.a: Two papers.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when stopping the game?
qa.a: Parul felt restless and irritable, a sign of dependence.

qa.q: What choice inside the story started Parul's recovery?
qa.a: Going to the student counselling centre that week after failing two papers.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel seeing Parul recover?
qa.a: Parveen is likely relieved and glad she spoke up early.

grounding: A young adult tells how a gaming dependence loop developed and how Parul exited it with help.

passage:
I'm Ojas, and Sahil and I shared a room in the hostel. Last year I watched him get hooked on vaping.
At first it was one at parties. Then in the room, then in the washroom between classes. If he didn't have it, he was snappy. He spent his mess money on refills.
One night he couldn't sleep without it and was pacing. He said, "I think I can't stop."
The next day he went to the campus health centre. The doctor explained how nicotine creates cravings and gave him a quitting plan. He threw out his vape in front of me.
The first week was rough; he chewed gum constantly and was grumpy. I don't know exactly what he felt, but he kept going.

qa.q: What did Sahil spend his mess money on?
qa.a: Refills.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling when he said he couldn't stop?
qa.a: Sahil was probably scared and frustrated, realising he was dependent.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that others trying to quit could learn from?
qa.a: He admitted the problem, got help from the health centre and followed a quitting plan.

qa.q: How does Ojas see Sahil's first week of quitting?
qa.a: Ojas sees it as rough and grumpy but notices Sahil kept going.

grounding: A roommate observes a young adult's vaping dependence and his effort to quit with medical help.

passage:
Week 1: Chaitanya downloaded a cricket betting app "just for fun" during the season. He won a little on the first night and texted Seema, "Easy money."
Week 4: He was on it every night, chasing losses, hiding his phone when Seema came over. He'd borrowed from two friends. He snapped at her when she asked what was wrong.
Week 6: Seema found him sitting on his bike outside the hostel at midnight, shaking. "I keep telling myself one more win and I'll stop. It never happens."
She didn't lecture. She said, "This is a loop, not a character flaw. Let's get you out."
That night he deleted the app and blocked his card for betting sites. The next morning he told his elder brother and called a gambling helpline number from the college counselling centre, with Seema sitting beside him.

qa.q: What kind of app did Chaitanya download?
qa.a: A cricket betting app.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling at midnight in week 6?

qa.q: What steps helped Chaitanya start to exit the loop, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the app, blocking betting on his card, telling his brother and calling a helpline, because they cut off access and brought in support.

passage:
Trisha, you asked why I don't drink at weddings. Let me tell you.
In my second year of college, I started drinking at hostel parties to feel less shy. Then before parties, to get ready. Then alone, on Sunday nights, to stop feeling anxious about Monday. I told myself I was fine because I still got good marks.
One morning I woke up and couldn't remember how I'd got back to my room. My roommate, Nisha, was sitting on her bed, waiting. She said, "I was really scared last night."
That did it. I went to the college counsellor that week. She helped me see the loop: anxiety, drink, relief, worse anxiety. I joined a support group and found other ways to calm down: running, and calling my sister.
It took more than a year. So when your Shreya Mausi says no thanks, that's why.

qa.q: What was Shreya's roommate's name?
qa.a: Nisha.

qa.q: How did young Shreya feel when she couldn't remember getting back to her room?
qa.a: Young Shreya felt frightened and shaken, realising things had gone too far.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why?
qa.a: Nisha saying she was scared, because it showed Shreya the harm to others and led her to the counsellor that week.

qa.q: What was that night like for Nisha?
qa.a: Nisha was probably terrified and helpless, sitting up waiting for her friend to wake.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recounting how drinking became a dependence loop in college and how she got out with help.

passage:
Mahima had three days left before her final exams, and she couldn't stop playing an online strategy game. Every time she opened her notes, her hand went to the laptop. "One match" became four hours. She was sleeping at 5 a.m. The hostel was quiet, her phone full of game alerts, and there was no one to stop her.
On the second night, her roommate Sonali found her crying at the desk. "I can't stop. I've tried."
Sonali didn't laugh. "Okay. What if I keep your laptop in my locker till Friday? And we study in the library together?"
Mahima hesitated. It felt childish. Then she handed it over and deleted the game from her phone.
The first day her hands kept reaching for nothing. By Friday she'd slept properly twice. After the exams, she booked an appointment with the college counsellor to work out why the game had such a hold.

qa.q: Where did Sonali offer to keep Mahima's laptop?
qa.a: In her locker till Friday.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Sonali found her?
qa.a: Mahima felt helpless and ashamed, crying because she couldn't stop despite trying.

qa.q: Why was handing over the laptop and seeing a counsellor a good combination?
qa.a: Removing access got her through the exams, and the counsellor can help her understand and change the loop for the long term.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt finding Mahima crying at the desk?
qa.a: Sonali was probably worried and sympathetic, and wanted to offer practical help rather than judgement.

grounding: Shows a young adult caught in a gaming dependence loop under exam pressure and taking steps, with help, to exit it.

passage: At 3:40 a.m. Indu's thumb was still tapping. One more match, she had said at midnight, and at one, and at two. The game dropped a small glittering chest after every win, and she could feel the itch for the next one before the current one ended. In the morning she missed her 9 a.m. lab for the third time that month. Her lab partner Kamal texted, "You alive? Sir asked about you." Indu stared at the message, then at her screen time: nine hours yesterday. Something cold went through her. That afternoon she deleted the game and asked Kamal to change her account password and keep it. By midnight her hand still reached for the phone. So the next day she booked a slot with the college counsellor, and told Kamal the plain truth: "Wake me for lab."

qa.q: How much screen time did Indu's phone show for the day before?
qa.a: It showed nine hours yesterday.

qa.q: What did Indu feel when she saw her screen time?
qa.a: Something cold went through her, a jolt of alarm and shame at how much the game had taken over.

qa.q: Why was seeing a counsellor a wise next step even after deleting the game?
qa.a: Her hand still reached for the phone at midnight, so the pull was stronger than willpower alone, and a professional can help her break the loop.

qa.q: How does Kamal see Indu's missed labs?
qa.a: Kamal seems worried rather than judging, checking in with "You alive?" and passing on that Sir asked about her.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising a gaming dependence loop and taking steps, including professional help, to exit it.
